title: Introduction to the C Programming Language
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and role of introduction to the c programming language in a C program.
Identify the relevant C language constructs, standard-library facilities or toolchain responsibilities.
Read a focused example and explain its data flow and control flow.
Recognize common errors, portability concerns and safety considerations for this topic.
Apply the concept in a small C program and verify it with compiler diagnostics and tests.

understand.concept: C is a general-purpose, procedural programming language used to write software that needs direct control over data representation, memory and program execution. It is commonly used in operating-system components, embedded systems, compilers, libraries and performance-sensitive applications. C source code is translated by an implementation toolchain into an executable or another target form; a browser does not execute C source directly.
understand.whyItMatters: Learning C develops a precise understanding of types, memory, control flow and how programs interact with their environment. These ideas are useful beyond C because they make it easier to reason about performance, resource ownership, data layout and lower-level system behaviour.
understand.analogy: Think of a C program as a set of precise instructions that must be translated for a particular machine and execution environment.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the formal C language rules, object lifetimes, types or implementation-defined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
A C program is written as source text and processed by a toolchain. A typical hosted implementation preprocesses directives, compiles source into object code, links required libraries and produces an executable. The exact commands and intermediate files depend on the compiler and platform. At run time, the operating system loads the program and the C runtime establishes the environment expected by the program.

C is often described as procedural because programs are commonly organized around functions that operate on data. The language also provides structures, pointers, arrays, enumerations and other mechanisms for expressing data relationships. It does not automatically manage dynamically allocated memory for the programmer: the program must follow clear ownership and lifetime rules.

C is standardized by ISO/IEC. Compiler implementations may support different language versions and extensions, so portable programs should identify their intended language standard and avoid relying on undocumented behaviour. A correct C program must respect the language rules; code that appears to work on one machine may still contain undefined behaviour.

examples.title: A first hosted C program
examples.explanation: The program includes the standard input/output declarations, defines the required main entry point for a hosted program, writes a line and returns a success status.

examples.title: A function and explicit data flow
examples.explanation: The square function receives an int value and returns an int. main calls it and checks the result. This illustrates function-based decomposition without relying on global state.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small program with main that prints your name and one sentence about what you want to build. Compile it with a C compiler, run it, and explain the role of the include directive, main, the output call and return value.
practise.independentTask: Create a program with two functions: one returns the larger of two integers and the other prints a short report. Test equal values, negative values and values near the range limits of int. Record the compiler and language standard used.
hints: C source is not HTML, CSS or JavaScript; it needs a C compiler toolchain.
A hosted C program normally starts execution in main.
Include files provide declarations; they do not paste a complete executable library into the source.
Prefer standard, portable language features unless a platform-specific extension is deliberately required.
Undefined behaviour is not a predictable error message; the program has no guaranteed result after it occurs.
